card.title: Arguments vs evidence — spotting the fallacy

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A claim is not an argument until evidence and reasoning link them; data without interpretation proves nothing, and interpretation without data persuades nobody. Critical thinking dissects debates into claim → evidence → warrant → rebuttal, then stress-tests each joint: sample size, correlation vs causation, sweeping quantifiers ('everybody'), missing voices. Literary analysis is the same surgery on texts — interpretation anchored in quoted moments.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: argument = claim + evidence + warrant (the link)  ·  fallacy scan: hasty generalisation ('everybody…') · false cause (phones⇢scores?) · sweeping 'so…will' predictions · missing counter-evidence  ·  data answers need: sample, comparison, confounds, conclusion-scope

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Critique the reasoning, never just the conclusion — a true claim can still be badly argued. Survey data (400 students, phones vs performance) speaks only with confounds controlled (study hours? school type?). Literary interpretation needs textual moments; unquoted readings are opinions.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: 'Everybody concentrates better without phones, so banning them will…' (NEB 2023, 5 marks): 'everybody' is unmeasured, the causal jump from correlation to ban is unearned — the answer names the generalisation and demands the missing evidence. The 2022 survey task reverses it: GIVEN data, reason carefully to scoped conclusions (compare groups, note confounds, resist overclaim).

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Debate teardown: (1) isolate the claim (ban phones); (2) list offered evidence (asserted concentration gain — no data cited); (3) name the gaps (hasty generalisation via 'everybody', correlation/causation blur, no counter-case like educational phone use); (4) verdict: unproven as stated + what evidence WOULD prove it (controlled comparison). Four moves, full marks (NEB 2023 pattern).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Fallacy-spotting is not refutation — naming 'hasty generalisation' does not make the claim false, only unsupported. Data analysis cannot fix bad data (biased sample, loaded questions). Literary readings stay plural: two well-evidenced interpretations can both stand.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: From survey to conclusion, step by step: describe the sample (who, how many) → compare the right groups (phone-heavy vs phone-light, matched otherwise) → check confounds (what else differs?) → scope the claim ('among THESE students' not 'all students') → state what further data would confirm. Each step is one mark; skipping confounds is the classic lost mark.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Underline quantifiers (all/everybody/never = red flags), causal verbs (proves/causes vs suggests/linked), and missing numbers. Data questions: sample → comparison → confound → scope. Always end with the verdict PLUS the evidence that would change it.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: NEB 2023 (5): mobile-ban debate — evaluate the argument (generalisation, evidence gaps). NEB 2022 (5): 400-student phone-vs-performance survey — reasoned answers with scoped conclusions. Literary-analysis readings follow claim→moment→technique→purpose.
